questions.q: Why do training and inference typically need genuinely different multi-region strategies?
options: Training can run wherever GPU capacity and training data already are, while inference needs to be near users because every network hop adds to latency a real caller feels
Training always requires more regions than inference
Inference never has any latency requirements
Training and inference must always run in the exact same region by cloud provider rule
questions.explain: Training is a batch-shaped problem nobody waits on in real time, so it can run wherever capacity and data are; inference is a request/response problem where latency to the user matters directly.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should drive the choice of region for a training run, in roughly this order?
options: Only which region has the cheapest electricity, with no other factor
GPU capacity/SKU availability, then where the training data already lives, then cost
Only which region the company's headquarters is in
Only user proximity to the training cluster
questions.explain: User proximity barely factors into training placement; what matters is where the needed GPU capacity exists, where the data already lives, and cost once those narrow the field.

questions.q: What is 'data gravity' in the context of choosing where training should run?
options: A rule that GPUs must be physically stacked by weight
A billing discount for keeping data in one region
The tendency for compute to be pulled toward where large datasets already live, because repeatedly moving the data is slow and costly
A requirement that model weights be stored on disk, not in VRAM
questions.explain: Data gravity describes why training often runs where its data already sits, rather than moving large datasets to wherever compute happens to be cheapest.

questions.q: What does a global traffic routing layer, like Azure Front Door/Traffic Manager or AWS Global Accelerator, do for a multi-region inference deployment?
options: It trains the model across multiple regions simultaneously
It eliminates the need for any regional inference deployment at all
It replaces the need for GPU capacity planning
It directs each caller to the nearest healthy regional inference endpoint instead of one fixed central destination
questions.explain: A global routing layer sends traffic to whichever healthy regional deployment is nearest to that caller, which is the mechanism that makes a multi-region inference strategy actually reduce latency.

questions.q: What can force training and inference for a given dataset into the same region, overriding both GPU-availability and user-latency reasoning?
options: A data residency requirement that mandates certain data, and the compute touching it, stay within a specific jurisdiction
A preference for using fewer cloud regions to simplify billing
The fact that Kubernetes clusters cannot span regions
A requirement that all model weights be stored in FP32
questions.explain: Regulatory data residency requirements can force both the training data's compute and the inference endpoint serving it to stay in-region, regardless of where capacity is cheapest or where most users are.
